etymology: Anglo-Saxon exclamation of address, unchanged in form since Old English — an unmodified cry that arrests attention before a summons, invitation, or alarm is spoken.
biblical_def:
Turn aside, sit down here. Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters. Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north.

Ho is Scripture's herald-word, the sound made before the sentence that matters is spoken. Boaz uses it at the gate of Bethlehem to stop the unnamed kinsman in his path and open the legal proceeding that will make Ruth his wife and preserve the line of David — a summons, not a greeting. Isaiah uses the same cry to open the gospel's freest invitation: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, an offer of wine and milk without money and without price, addressed to those who have nothing to bring but their thirst. Zechariah doubles the cry — Ho, ho — to rouse the exiles still comfortable in Babylon to flee before the LORD moves against the nations that scattered them. In every case Ho precedes an action God's people must take: turn aside, come and buy, flee. It is not small talk. It is the sound of heaven demanding to be heard before it will be answered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), HO: an exclamation used to excite attention, or to give notice of approach; a call to arrest the hearer before the substance of the message is spoken.
webster_full: HO, exclam. A word used in calling, or to give notice of approach, or to excite attention.
Used also as a sea-term, to hail a ship, or to check the speed of a course.
An interjection of pure address, without independent grammatical content of its own.
In Scripture usage, precedes a legal summons (Ruth), a gospel invitation (Isaiah), and a prophetic alarm (Zechariah).
Distinguished from Woe, a kindred interjection of lament and judgment rather than summons.
scriptures: Rut 4:1

Then went Boaz up to the gate, and sat him down there: and, behold, the kinsman of whom Boaz spake came by; unto whom he said, Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here. And he turned aside, and sat down.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Zec 2:6
Ho, ho, come forth, and flee from the land of the north, saith the LORD: for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heaven, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Seeker-sensitive gospel presentations soften Isaiah 55's Ho into a casual icebreaker rather than a herald's summons, flattening the paradox of a costly gift freely offered into a generic affirmation of come-as-you-are religion.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern invitation culture reads Ho, every one that thirsteth as a warm, low-stakes welcome and stops there, detaching the cry from what follows it: an effectual summons to those whom God himself has made to thirst, calling them to buy at a price Christ alone has paid. The verse is not a general affirmation of every seeker's autonomous journey; it is the LORD's own herald-cry, sovereignly addressed, answered only by those he has first made to thirst.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Ho is not decoration; Boaz's legal summons at the gate and the LORD's gospel summons in Isaiah share one register — a word that commands hearing before it offers anything, and a hearing that is itself God's gift.
roots_summary: The Hebrew interjection behind two of the three occurrences is the same cry that opens the prophets' woe-oracles elsewhere in the Old Testament, showing Ho and Woe as two English renderings of one summons-word.
roots_lines: Ho in Ruth 4 is Boaz's legal summons that opens the kinsman-redemption of Ruth.
Ho in Isaiah 55 is the LORD's own herald-cry opening the gospel's freest invitation.
Ho, ho doubled in Zechariah 2 is an alarm rousing exiles to flee before judgment falls.
In every occurrence the cry precedes an action required of the hearer, not mere information.
The same Hebrew interjection stands behind the prophets' woe-oracles elsewhere in the canon.
usage: Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here — Boaz's summons that opens the redemption of Ruth.
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters — the gospel's freest invitation.
Ho, ho, come forth, and flee — the alarm rousing exiles before judgment falls on Babylon.

etymology: Middle English pissen, from Old French pissier — a plain Anglo-Saxon-register bodily verb the Authorized Version does not euphemize, carried into the fixed idiom him that pisseth against the wall.
biblical_def:
Him that pisseth against the wall. Him that is shut up and left in Israel. Cut off from Jeroboam him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel.

The phrase him that pisseth against the wall is a fixed Hebrew idiom for any male, from the plainest and most physical mark of manhood — used without embarrassment because the judgment it introduces is total. David swears by it in his oath against Nabal's household; Ahijah, Jehu, and Elijah use it in near-identical form to pronounce the extermination of the houses of Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab, each paired with him that is shut up and left, meaning every male, bond or free, down to the last. The KJV's plain translation preserves the Hebrew's own bluntness rather than softening it, and that bluntness is doing theological work: it says these royal houses are not being merely defeated but wiped out to the last man, a totality the softer English of later versions can obscure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PISS: to discharge urine; a plain Saxon verb, here inflected in the archaic third-person singular ending -eth, as in doeth, giveth, walketh.
webster_full: PISS, v.i. To discharge urine.
PISS, v.t. To discharge from the bladder; as, to piss blood.
PISSETH, the archaic third-person singular present, as walketh from walk, doeth from do.
The fixed idiom him that pisseth against the wall denotes any male, without distinction of rank.
Paired in each occurrence with him that is shut up and left, together meaning every male without exception.
scriptures: So and more also do God unto the enemies of David, if I leave of all that pertain to him by the morning light any that pisseth against the wall.

Therefore, behold, I will bring evil upon the house of Jeroboam, and will cut off from Jeroboam him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel, and will take away the remnant of the house of Jeroboam, as a man taketh away dung, till it be all gone.
Behold, I will bring evil upon thee, and will take away thy posterity, and will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel,
For the whole house of Ahab shall perish: and I will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel:
corruption_summary: Modern squeamishness about the KJV's bodily plainness leads some readers to treat the phrase as a translation error or an embarrassment to be silently updated, when in fact its bluntness is precisely what conveys the totality of the judgment pronounced.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary sensibility, trained to expect Scripture's English to be tidy and dignified throughout, flinches at a verse like this and sometimes concludes the Authorized Version has simply erred toward vulgarity where a smoother modern rendering would be more reverent. This gets the translators' aim backward: the Hebrew idiom is itself blunt, and a Bible that sands down every physical bluntness of the original text trades fidelity for a false decorum Scripture itself does not observe.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical plainness of speech, rightly used, serves the text's own gravity — the totality of covenant judgment against Jeroboam's, Baasha's, and Ahab's houses is felt precisely because the idiom leaves no dignified male untouched by it.
roots_summary: The Hebrew idiom rendered pisseth against the wall (mashtin b'qir) is a set legal-covenantal formula for every male, used four times in the historical books to pronounce total dynastic judgment.
roots_lines: Pisseth against the wall first appears in David's own oath against the household of Nabal.
Ahijah repeats the exact phrase to pronounce the end of Jeroboam's dynasty.
Jehu's messenger applies it to Baasha's house before Elijah applies it again to Ahab's.
In every case it is paired with shut up and left, together meaning every male without exception.
The KJV's plain rendering preserves an idiom later versions typically soften to males or every male.
usage: So and more also do God unto the enemies of David — David's oath against Nabal's household.
Him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left — total dynastic judgment.
Repeated against Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab — the same formula for the end of a royal house.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon ofer (over) + flowan (to flow) — the older strong past participle of overflow, displaced in modern English by overflowed but retained in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
When it had overflown all his banks. Whose foundation was overflown with a flood. With the arms of a flood shall they be overflown.

Overflown gathers three very different floods under one word. The mighty men who cross the Jordan to David at Ziklag do so when it had overflown all his banks — the river at full spring spate, a natural obstacle their loyalty refuses to be stopped by. Job's friend Eliphaz uses the same word for the wicked, whose foundation was overflown with a flood, God's judgment pictured as an inundation that sweeps away everything a man has built his life on. Daniel's vision applies it a third way, to an invading army: with the arms of a flood shall they be overflown, the language of a river turned into the language of war. Scripture's overflown moves, in three verses, from a literal river crossed by the faithful, to a metaphorical flood of judgment on the wicked, to a flood of armies sweeping over nations — one word carrying nature, judgment, and history at once.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from OVERFLOW: to flow over; to cover with water or other fluid, as land not usually covered; the older strong participle, now largely replaced by overflowed.
webster_full: OVERFLOW, v.t. To spread over; to cover with water or other fluid.
OVERFLOW, v.i. To run over, as a stream or vessel; to be superabundant.
OVERFLOWN, the older strong past participle, as flown from fly, now largely displaced by overflowed.
Applied literally to the Jordan at flood stage, and figuratively to judgment and invasion.
The imagery of an overflowing flood is a standing biblical figure for sudden, sweeping judgment.
scriptures: These are they that went over Jordan in the first month, when it had overflown all his banks; and they put to flight all them of the valleys, both toward the east, and toward the west.
Which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overflown with a flood:
And with the arms of a flood shall they be overflown from before him, and shall be broken; yea, also the prince of the covenant.
corruption_summary: Treating the Jordan crossing in 1 Chronicles 12 as mere adventure-narrative color, rather than as evidence entered for the mighty men's covenant loyalty to David, misses why the Chronicler bothers to mention the river's condition at all.
corruption_paragraphs: A purely literary reading of 1 Chronicles 12 can pass over when it had overflown all his banks as incidental scene-setting. The Chronicler's own purpose is theological: these are men counted worthy of remembrance precisely because they came to David through danger, at flood stage, when a lesser loyalty would have waited for the water to fall.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's floods are never merely meteorological — the same word that describes a river at spring spate describes the LORD's judgment sweeping over the wicked and armies sweeping over nations, one figure doing triple duty across the canon.
roots_summary: Overflown preserves the older strong past participle pattern seen in flown, grown, and known, a form English has since regularized toward the weak -ed ending in most verbs but the Authorized Version retains throughout.
roots_lines: Overflown in 1 Chronicles 12 describes the Jordan at full spring flood, crossed by David's mighty men.
Overflown in Job 22 pictures a wicked man's whole foundation swept away by judgment.
Overflown in Daniel 11 turns the same flood-image into a figure for an invading army.
In every case the word marks a force too great to be resisted by ordinary means.
The strong participle form (rather than overflowed) is characteristic of the Authorized Version's older English.
usage: When it had overflown all his banks — the Jordan at flood, crossed by David's loyal mighty men.
Whose foundation was overflown with a flood — judgment pictured as an inundation on the wicked.
With the arms of a flood shall they be overflown — an invading army as a sweeping flood.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon siexteoda, the ordinal of sixteen — sixteenth appears in the Authorized Version chiefly in the courses of the priests and Levites appointed by David and confirmed at Hezekiah's reformation.
biblical_def:
The fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer. The sixteenth to Hananiah, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve. In the sixteenth day of the first month they made an end.

Sixteenth marks two very different moments of ordered service. In 1 Chronicles 24, it names the sixteenth of twenty-four priestly courses cast by lot under David, so that no family's turn at the altar depended on favor or seniority but on the LORD's own disposal by lot. In chapter 25, the sixteenth course belongs to the singers under Hananiah, the same lot-cast order extended from sacrifice to song, both alike ministering before the LORD. In 2 Chronicles 29, the number moves from assignment to accomplishment: on the sixteenth day of the first month, Hezekiah's priests finish cleansing the temple Ahaz had defiled, a task begun on the first day of the month and completed, to the day, sixteen days later. The same ordinal that orders worship by lot also marks the day worship was finally restored.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), SIXTEENTH: the ordinal of sixteen; the sixth after the tenth; noting the order of one of sixteen or more things.
webster_full: SIXTEENTH, a. The ordinal of sixteen; the sixth after the tenth.
SIXTEENTH, n. The sixth part of sixteen equal parts of a thing.
In 1 Chronicles 24-25 the ordinal numbers the twenty-four priestly and Levitical courses cast by lot.
In 2 Chronicles 29 the ordinal marks a calendar day, the completion of the temple's cleansing.
The device of casting lots for the sixteenth course, like every course, removed human preference from priestly assignment.
scriptures: The fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer,
The sixteenth to Hananiah, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve:

Now they began on the first day of the first month to sanctify, and on the eighth day of the month came they to the porch of the LORD: so they sanctified the house of the LORD in eight days; and in the sixteenth day of the first month they made an end.
corruption_summary: Skeptical readings dismiss the priestly and Levitical course-lists of 1 Chronicles 24-25 as tedious postexilic bureaucratic invention rather than historical record; the confessional reading takes them as a real, divinely-ordered rota David actually established.
corruption_paragraphs: A historical-critical approach to Chronicles treats these long lists of courses, cast by lot down to the sixteenth and beyond, as a later priestly class's retrojection of its own organization onto David, without independent historical value. The text presents the lots as cast in the actual presence of David, the princes, the priests, and the Levites, a real historical ordering event, not a literary fiction.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God orders even the rotation of ordinary priestly duty by lot rather than by human preference, and that same care for order stands behind Hezekiah's insistence on finishing the temple's cleansing to the day rather than leaving reformation half done.
roots_summary: The twenty-four courses established in 1 Chronicles 24-25, sixteenth among them, remained the working schedule of temple service into the New Testament era — Zacharias was serving in the course of Abia when the angel announced John the Baptist's birth (Luke 1:5-8).
roots_lines: Sixteenth in 1 Chronicles 24 names Immer's course among the twenty-four priestly courses cast by lot.
Sixteenth in 1 Chronicles 25 names Hananiah's course among the Levitical singers, ordered the same way.
Sixteenth in 2 Chronicles 29 marks the calendar day Hezekiah's priests finished cleansing the temple.
The same course-system, established under David, was still operating in Zacharias's day (Luke 1:5).
Casting lots for each course, sixteenth included, kept priestly assignment free of human favoritism.
usage: The fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer — priestly courses cast by lot under David.
The sixteenth to Hananiah — the Levitical singers' courses, ordered the same way as the priests'.
In the sixteenth day of the first month they made an end — Hezekiah's temple cleansing finished to the day.

etymology: Compound of women + servants — the Authorized Version's counterpart to menservants, together rendering the fixed Hebrew pair for male and female household bondservants.
biblical_def:
Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants, and gave them unto Abraham. I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants. He rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants.

Womenservants names the female counterpart of the patriarchal household's bondservants, always paired in Scripture with menservants as two halves of one social category. Abimelech restores Sarah to Abraham with a gift that includes womenservants, a king's acknowledgment of wrong done and a gesture of peace. Jacob, reporting his own prosperity to Esau before their reunion, lists womenservants alongside oxen, asses, and flocks as part of the substance God has given him in Laban's house. And when Jacob finally crosses the ford Jabbok, it is his two wives and his two womenservants — Zilpah and Bilhah, the mothers of four of the twelve tribes — that he takes over first, household order preserved even in the night he wrestles with God. The word marks real persons bound within the patriarchal household economy, never mere property in the text's own moral accounting, however plainly the ancient social structure differs from the modern one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SERVANT: one who serves; a compound noun paired with menservants to denote female household bondservants under the patriarchal economy.
webster_full: SERVANT, n. A person who attends another, and acts at his command.
WOMENSERVANTS, the plural compound denoting female bondservants of a household.
Regularly paired with menservants as the two halves of a patriarch's household staff.
Distinguished in the text from wives, sons, and daughters, though bound within the same household.
Named among the marks of a patriarch's substance or prosperity, alongside flocks and herds.
scriptures: And Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants, and gave them unto Abraham, and restored him Sarah his wife.
Gen 32:5
And I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants: and I have sent to tell my lord, that I may find grace in thy sight.
And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok.
corruption_summary: Reading the patriarchal household's menservants and womenservants through the lens of modern chattel slavery, without distinguishing the ancient Near Eastern household-bondservant economy from that later institution, obscures more than it clarifies about the text's own moral world.
corruption_paragraphs: A flattened equivalence between every ancient household-servant arrangement and the transatlantic slave trade reads later categories back into Genesis without regard for the very different legal and social structures involved — inheritance rights, eventual freedom, and household protection that shaped bondservice under the patriarchs. The text names Zilpah and Bilhah, two of Jacob's womenservants, as the mothers of Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, four of the twelve tribes, a status no flattened reading of servant accounts for.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture names real persons under real household structures without either romanticizing ancient bondservice or importing categories foreign to the text, and traces the LORD's own providence working through household arrangements very different from a modern reader's own.
roots_summary: Womenservants and menservants render a fixed Hebrew word-pair (avadim and shephachot) that recurs across the patriarchal narratives as the standard inventory-phrase for a household's full bondservant staff.
roots_lines: Womenservants first appears as part of Abimelech's restitution gift to Abraham after taking Sarah.
The same pair, menservants and womenservants, appears in Jacob's report of his prosperity to Esau.
Jacob's own two womenservants are named elsewhere as Zilpah and Bilhah, mothers of four tribes.
The word always appears paired with menservants, never standing for female persons generally.
The pairing functions in the text as a standard inventory-phrase for a household's full staff.
usage: Abimelech took sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and womenservants — a king's restitution to Abraham.
Oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants — Jacob's report of his own prosperity.
His two wives, and his two womenservants — Zilpah and Bilhah, crossing the ford Jabbok with Jacob.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of DELIVER)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of deliver, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version — thou deliveredst, alongside gavest, heardest, and broughtest.
biblical_def:
Thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies. Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents. Thou deliveredst unto me two talents.

Deliveredst carries two very different meanings under one archaic form. In Nehemiah's great covenant prayer, thou deliveredst is God's own act of judicial discipline — handing a rebellious Israel over to her enemies, the low point of a repeated cycle of sin, judgment, mercy, and deliverance the prayer traces across the whole Old Testament. In the parable of the talents, deliveredst is the master's act of trust, the same word now describing not judgment but a gift entrusted to a servant's stewardship, and Christ places the word in the mouths of the servants themselves as they give their account. One verb form, addressed to God in confession and echoed back to a master in accounting, binds together two of Scripture's central themes: the LORD who justly hands sinners to judgment, and the LORD who graciously entrusts gifts he will one day require an account of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DELIVER: to free; to release; to give, hand, or commit; here in the archaic second-person singular past, deliveredst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release from restraint, danger, or evil.
DELIVER, v.t. To give; to put into another's hand or power; to commit; to surrender.
DELIVEREDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as heardest, gavest.
In Nehemiah 9 the sense is judicial: God handing a rebellious people to their enemies.
In Matthew 25 the sense is entrustment: a master committing talents to a servant's stewardship.
scriptures: Neh 9:27

Therefore thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies, who vexed them: and in the time of their trouble, when they cried unto thee, thou heardest them from heaven; and according to thy manifold mercies thou gavest them saviours, who saved them out of the hand of their enemies.
And so he that had received five talents came and brought other five talents, saying, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more.
He also that had received two talents came and said, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me two talents: behold, I have gained two other talents beside them.
corruption_summary: Reading Nehemiah 9's cycle of sin and deliverance as merely a literary pattern of ancient Israelite self-understanding, rather than a true theological account of God's actual dealings in history, empties the prayer of its confessional force.
corruption_paragraphs: A purely literary-critical reading treats the recurring pattern in Nehemiah 9 — rebellion, deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies, cries for mercy, gavest them saviours — as a redactor's theological schema imposed on unrelated historical episodes, rather than the Levites' own true confession before the covenant-renewing assembly. The prayer is offered as history and as present confession at once, not as literary device.

The corrective is to hold the parable's full weight: the same verb that names God's judicial handing-over in Nehemiah also names the trust a master places in a servant in Matthew 25, and both stewardship that gains and stewardship that hides its gift will be required to give account, thou deliveredst unto me being the very phrase each servant must answer for.
roots_summary: The -st ending on deliveredst belongs to a whole family of archaic second-person forms (gavest, heardest, broughtest) the Authorized Version uses consistently whenever thou is the subject, a grammatical feature now obsolete in ordinary English but still legible across the text.
roots_lines: Deliveredst in Nehemiah 9 names God's judicial act of handing a rebellious people to their enemies.
The same prayer pairs deliveredst with heardest and gavest in one repeated cycle of mercy and judgment.
Deliveredst in Matthew 25 shifts the sense to a master entrusting talents to a servant's care.
Christ places the word in the mouths of the faithful servants as they render their account.
One archaic verb form thus spans both divine judgment and divine entrustment in two Testaments.
usage: Thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies — God's judicial discipline in Nehemiah's prayer.
Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents — a servant's account of entrusted stewardship.
Thou deliveredst unto me two talents — the second servant's matching account before his master.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of PROMISE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of promise, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version, appearing chiefly in prayers that recall God's own spoken word back to him.
biblical_def:
That thou promisedst him: thou spakest also with thy mouth. That thou promisedst him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight. Promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land.

Promisedst is the verb of covenant prayer — never a man reminding God of a debt, but a man pleading God's own word back to him in confidence that he who spoke will perform. Solomon uses it twice in his temple dedication, kept with thy servant David my father that thou promisedst him, grounding the newly built house not in Solomon's achievement but in a promise God himself spoke and has now fulfilled with thine hand. Nehemiah's Levites use the same word in the great post-exilic prayer, tracing the promise of the land itself back to God's own sworn word to the fathers, the ground of every claim Israel has to Canaan. In both prayers, promisedst functions as an act of faith: to say thou promisedst is to stake everything on the character of the one who spoke, not on the speaker's own worthiness to receive it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PROMISE: to make a declaration to another, binding oneself to do or forbear some act; here in the archaic second-person singular past, promisedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: PROMISE, v.t. To make a declaration to another which binds the promiser to do, or forbear to do, some act.
PROMISE, n. A declaration which gives to the party to whom it is made a right to expect the performance of the act.
PROMISEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as spakest, gavest.
In 1 Kings 8 the word grounds Solomon's temple dedication in God's own spoken word to David.
In Nehemiah 9 the word grounds Israel's claim to the land in God's sworn oath to the fathers.
scriptures: Who hast kept with thy servant David my father that thou promisedst him: thou spakest also with thy mouth, and hast fulfilled it with thine hand, as it is this day.

Therefore now, LORD God of Israel, keep with thy servant David my father that thou promisedst him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit on the throne of Israel; so that thy children take heed to their way, that they walk before me as thou hast walked before me.
Neh 9:15

And gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger, and broughtest forth water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land which thou hadst sworn to give them.
corruption_summary: Treating biblical covenant promises as ancient Israel's own religious self-talk rather than God's actual binding word grounds the modern reader's confidence in nothing, when Solomon and the Levites both ground theirs in the LORD's spoken and sworn word alone.
corruption_paragraphs: A purely sociological reading of covenant language reduces thou promisedst to ancient Israel's way of narrating its own national self-confidence, a rhetorical convention rather than an appeal to an actual divine speech-act with binding force. Solomon's prayer explicitly distinguishes the two: thou spakest also with thy mouth, and hast fulfilled it with thine hand — a real word, really kept, not a national legend.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical prayer grounds its confidence entirely outside the one praying — in what God himself has spoken — and that pattern of pleading God's own promise back to him is the model for every believer's prayer, not a device unique to Solomon or Nehemiah's Levites.
roots_summary: Both occurrences pair promisedst with a verb of speech (spakest) or oath (sworn), underlining that biblical promise is never a vague hope but a specific spoken or sworn word God has bound himself to perform.
roots_lines: Promisedst in 1 Kings 8:24 grounds Solomon's temple dedication in a promise God spoke and fulfilled.
Promisedst in 1 Kings 8:25 becomes the basis of Solomon's plea for the continuance of David's line.
Promisedst in Nehemiah 9:15 grounds Israel's claim to Canaan in God's own sworn oath to the fathers.
In every case a human petitioner pleads God's own word back to him rather than personal merit.
The pattern models covenant prayer generally: confidence resting in the speaker's character, not the petitioner's.
usage: Kept with thy servant David that thou promisedst him — Solomon grounding the temple in God's word.
There shall not fail thee a man in my sight — the promise Solomon pleads for David's line to continue.
Promisedst them that they should go in to possess the land — Israel's claim to Canaan in Nehemiah's prayer.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of STAND)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of stand, formed with the -est ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version — thou stoodest, alongside knewest and sawest.
biblical_def:
I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me. The day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb. The day that thou stoodest on the other side.

Stoodest marks three very different postures before God. Balaam confesses it to the angel who has blocked his donkey's path, I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me, a diviner admitting he could not see what his own animal saw plainly. Moses uses the same word to recall Israel's own defining moment, the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb, the nation physically present at the giving of the law, a memory Deuteronomy repeatedly commands Israel not to forget. Obadiah turns the word against Edom, the day that thou stoodest on the other side, condemning a brother nation's passive complicity while Jerusalem fell, standing aside being itself a form of standing against. To stand, in each case, is never neutral: blocking a path, receiving the law, or watching a brother's ruin without helping are each a stoodest that God takes full account of.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from STAND: to be on the feet; to remain fixed in place; here in the archaic second-person singular past, stoodest, addressed to thou.
webster_full: STAND, v.i. To be upon the feet, as an animal; to remain erect.
STAND, v.i. To remain fixed in a place; to stop; to halt.
STOODEST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -est, as knewest, sawest.
In Numbers 22 the word names an angel's visible, physical opposition to Balaam's path.
In Obadiah the word extends to a nation's passive standing-aside, itself judged as a form of hostility.
scriptures: And Balaam said unto the angel of the LORD, I have sinned; for I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me: now therefore, if it displease thee, I will get me back again.
Deu 4:10

Specially the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb, when the LORD said unto me, Gather me the people together, and I will make them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and that they may teach their children.
Oba 1:11

In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces, and foreigners entered into his gates, and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even thou wast as one of them.
corruption_summary: Modern moral instinct treats bystanding as morally neutral unless a person actively participates in wrongdoing; Obadiah's oracle names Edom's mere standing-aside as itself a form of complicity that provokes the LORD's judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: A therapeutic-individualist ethic tends to locate moral failure only in direct action against another, leaving passive non-involvement as blameless. Obadiah will not allow it: thou stoodest on the other side, doing nothing while Jerusalem fell, is itself judged even thou wast as one of them — bystanding toward a brother's ruin is treated as brotherhood with his destroyers.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Deuteronomy 4's stoodest before the LORD at Horeb is meant to be remembered and retold precisely so it is never treated as mere history — a nation that once stood to receive the law is bound by that standing, generation after generation.
roots_summary: The archaic -est ending on stoodest belongs to the same grammatical family as knewest and sawest, marking the second-person singular past throughout the Authorized Version whenever thou is the addressed subject.
roots_lines: Stoodest in Numbers 22 names the angel's visible opposition Balaam himself had failed to perceive.
Stoodest in Deuteronomy 4 recalls Israel's own physical presence at the giving of the law at Horeb.
Stoodest in Obadiah 1 names Edom's passive complicity while Jerusalem fell to invaders.
In each case the standing described carries moral weight, never a neutral fact of posture.
Deuteronomy commands the memory of Horeb to be taught to children precisely so it is never forgotten.
usage: I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me — Balaam's confession to the angel of the LORD.
The day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb — Israel's defining memory of the law given.
The day that thou stoodest on the other side — Obadiah's judgment on Edom's complicit bystanding.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of TRUST)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of trust, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version — thou trustedst, appearing chiefly in oracles of judgment against misplaced confidence.
biblical_def:
Thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst. Thy fenced cities, wherein thou trustedst, with the sword. In the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee.

Trustedst is a word of exposed confidence, always naming something that failed the one who leaned on it. Moses warns Israel in advance that her own fenced walls, wherein thou trustedst, will come down under covenant curse if she breaks faith with the LORD. Jeremiah applies the identical judgment to Judah's fenced cities, the very fortifications the nation trusted for safety, falling to the sword because the nation trusted them instead of the LORD who built and could as easily unbuild them. And when Jeremiah complains that even in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, he is wearied, the LORD's answer is that greater trials are coming, sharper than any he has yet faced. In every occurrence, trustedst exposes a confidence misplaced in something other than the LORD himself — walls, cities, or a season of ease — each one shown, in the end, unable to bear the weight put on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TRUST: to place confidence in; to rely on the truth, faithfulness, or ability of; here in the archaic second-person singular past, trustedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: TRUST, v.t. To place confidence in; to rely on.
TRUST, n. Confidence; reliance on the integrity, ability, or character of a person or thing.
TRUSTEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as wantedst, hadst.
In Deuteronomy 28 and Jeremiah 5 the object of misplaced trust is fortified walls and cities.
In Jeremiah 12 the object of trust widens to a whole season or land of apparent peace and safety.
scriptures: And he shall besiege thee in all thy gates, until thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst, throughout all thy land: and he shall besiege thee in all thy gates throughout all thy land, which the LORD thy God hath given thee.
Jer 5:17

And they shall eat up thine harvest, and thy bread, which thy sons and thy daughters should eat: they shall eat up thy flocks and thine herds: they shall eat up thy vines and thy fig trees: they shall impoverish thy fenced cities, wherein thou trustedst, with the sword.
Jer 12:5

If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?
corruption_summary: Modern confidence in material security, institutions, and infrastructure runs on precisely the logic Deuteronomy 28 and Jeremiah condemn — trust placed in what can be fortified, stockpiled, or defended, rather than in the LORD who alone gives and can as easily remove such defenses.
corruption_paragraphs: A secular reading of ancient warfare treats fenced walls, wherein thou trustedst, as simply inadequate military technology overrun by a stronger enemy, with no theological content. The text insists otherwise: the walls fall specifically because Israel and Judah trusted them instead of the covenant LORD who had given them in the first place, and their fall is covenant curse, not mere strategic failure.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah 12's own question — if present ease already wearies a man's trust, how will he stand when the swelling of Jordan comes — a standing warning against building confidence on any peace less permanent than the LORD who alone does not fail.
roots_summary: The three occurrences trace one moral logic across two centuries of Israel's history: Moses warns of it in Deuteronomy, Jeremiah watches it fulfilled against Judah's own fenced cities, and applies the same logic personally to his own wearied trust in Jeremiah 12.
roots_lines: Trustedst in Deuteronomy 28 warns in advance that Israel's own fortified walls will fail under covenant curse.
Trustedst in Jeremiah 5 records that same warning fulfilled against Judah's fenced cities generations later.
Trustedst in Jeremiah 12 turns from national fortification to a prophet's own wearied personal confidence.
In every case the object trusted, not the trusting itself, is exposed as inadequate to bear the weight put on it.
The pattern moves from national defense to a single man's endurance, the same principle scaled down.
usage: Thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst — covenant curse falling on misplaced confidence.
Thy fenced cities, wherein thou trustedst, with the sword — Jeremiah watching the warning fulfilled.
The land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee — Jeremiah's own trust tested and found wanting.

etymology: Latin confundere (to pour together, mingle, confound), through Old French confus — a state of things or minds mixed together past the point of order or distinction.
biblical_def:
The battle of the warrior is with confused noise. The assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.

Confused names a state where order has broken down past recognition, in two very different scenes. Isaiah's messianic prophecy contrasts the confused noise of ordinary warfare — garments rolled in blood, the chaos every battle before Christ has produced — with the child to be born, whose kingdom will end that pattern in burning and fuel of fire, judgment that finally silences the noise rather than adding to it. Luke's confused assembly at Ephesus is confusion of a different kind: a mob stirred up by Demetrius the silversmith against Paul's preaching, so disordered that the more part knew not wherefore they were come together, noise without any shared purpose at all. Set side by side, Scripture's two confusions are the world's normal condition apart from Christ — the confused violence nations inflict on one another, and the confused mob that gathers against the gospel without even knowing why — both answered not by more explanation but by the ordering, judging reign of the Prince of Peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONFUSE: to mix or blend so that things cannot be distinguished; disorder; a tumultuous or disordered state of things or persons.
webster_full: CONFUSE, v.t. To mix or blend, so as to render the separate parts indistinct.
CONFUSE, v.t. To disturb the mind or intellect by a suffusion of ideas.
CONFUSED, a. Mixed; blended without order; tumultuous; indistinct.
In Isaiah 9 the confused noise of battle is set against the ordered, everlasting kingdom of the child born.
In Acts 19 a confused assembly names a mob whose members cannot even state why they have gathered.
scriptures: Isa 9:5
For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire.
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
corruption_summary: Postmodern thought treats confusion and instability as the honest default condition of meaning itself, something to be inhabited rather than resolved; Scripture presents confusion as a disordered departure from God's own order, met and ended by the reign of Christ, not affirmed as authentic.
corruption_paragraphs: A postmodern sensibility that prizes ambiguity and resists settled meaning can read confused noise or a confused assembly almost sympathetically, as if disorder itself were a kind of honesty about how the world really is. Isaiah's prophecy will not allow that reading: the confused noise of every battle before Christ is explicitly contrasted with, and answered by, the ordered, burning judgment of the child whose government shall have no end (Isa 9:6-7) — confusion is the problem the Messiah's reign solves, not a condition to be affirmed.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Luke's own quiet irony in Acts 19: a mob raised in the name of religious and commercial zeal against the gospel cannot even say why it has gathered, confusion following naturally wherever the truth of Christ is resisted rather than received.
roots_summary: The Greek word behind confused in Acts 19 (sygcheo, to pour together) is the same root that gives English confusion generally, and stands in deliberate contrast to the good order the New Testament repeatedly commends in the church's own gatherings (1 Cor 14:33, 40).
roots_lines: Confused in Isaiah 9 names the noise of ordinary warfare, contrasted with the Messiah's ordered reign.
Confused in Acts 19 names a mob at Ephesus stirred up against Paul's preaching of the gospel.
In Acts, the confusion is so total that most present cannot say why they have gathered at all.
Isaiah 9's confused noise is explicitly answered by burning and fuel of fire, judgment ending disorder.
The New Testament elsewhere commends good order in the church's gatherings as the opposite of confusion.
usage: The battle of the warrior is with confused noise — ordinary warfare, before Isaiah's promised King.
This shall be with burning and fuel of fire — the Messiah's reign answering confusion with judgment.
The assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together — Ephesus's mob.
